Controls the Linux Audit system, allowing you to define rules that log security-relevant events like file access.
Displays the current SELinux mode, which can be Enforcing, Permissive or Disabled.
Shows detailed SELinux status, including the mode and loaded policy.
Displays the status of AppArmor profiles that restrict what programs are allowed to do.
Manages log files by rotating, compressing and deleting old logs automatically. It prevents logs from filling the disk.
Adds a message to the system log from the command line or scripts. It is useful for recording events.

Cyber Threats.definition: A social engineering attack in which attackers trick users into revealing sensitive information through deceptive messages or websites. Attackers often copy the logos and wording of trusted organizations and create a sense of urgency, and the stolen details are then used for fraud or further attacks.
Cyber Threats.example: A fake bank email asking a user to verify their account through a malicious link.

Cyber Threats.definition: A targeted phishing attack designed for a specific individual or organization. Because the message uses personal details gathered from social media or earlier breaches, it appears far more believable than mass phishing and has a higher success rate.
Cyber Threats.example: An attacker sends a fake email using an employee's name and workplace details to steal login credentials.

Cyber Threats.definition: A phishing attack specifically targeting high-level executives or important individuals. These messages are carefully written to look like legal, financial or board-level communication, since the victim has the authority to approve payments or access sensitive data.
Cyber Threats.example: A fake financial approval request sent to a company's CEO.

Cyber Threats.definition: A phishing attack conducted through SMS text messages. Short messages and shortened links make it hard to spot the deception on a phone, and the messages often claim to be about deliveries, banking alerts or prizes.
Cyber Threats.example: A fake delivery message asking someone to click a link and pay a small fee.

Cyber Threats.definition: A social engineering attack that uses voice calls to trick victims into sharing sensitive information. Callers may spoof the phone number and use pressure or fear to rush the victim, so banks advise never sharing PINs or one-time passwords over a call.
Cyber Threats.example: Someone pretending to be a bank employee and requesting an OTP over the phone.

Cyber Threats.definition: Malicious software that encrypts a victim's files or systems and demands payment for their recovery. Attackers often threaten to leak the stolen data as well, so organizations rely on offline backups, patching and user awareness to reduce the impact.
Cyber Threats.example: WannaCry infected computers and encrypted their files.

Cyber Threats.definition: Malicious software that secretly monitors user activities and collects information. It can capture passwords, messages, location and browsing habits, and it often arrives bundled with free software or through malicious links.
Cyber Threats.example: A program secretly recording browsing activity and sending it to an attacker.

Cyber Threats.definition: Software that displays unwanted advertisements and may track user activity. While some adware is only annoying, aggressive versions can slow the device, change browser settings and expose users to malicious websites.
Cyber Threats.example: A suspicious application displaying continuous pop-up advertisements.

Cyber Threats.definition: Malware that disguises itself as legitimate software to trick users into installing it. Unlike viruses, trojans do not replicate by themselves; they rely on tricking the user, and once installed they may steal data, open a backdoor or download more malware.
Cyber Threats.example: A fake software installer that secretly installs malicious code.

Cyber Threats.definition: Malware that independently replicates and spreads across systems or networks. Worms need no user action or host file, so they can spread extremely fast, consume bandwidth and carry harmful payloads such as ransomware.
Cyber Threats.example: A network worm exploiting vulnerable computers to spread automatically.

Cyber Threats.definition: Malicious code that attaches itself to legitimate files or programs and spreads when they are executed. A virus needs a host file and some user action to spread, and it may corrupt data, slow the system or deliver other malicious functions.
Cyber Threats.example: An infected document that spreads malicious code when opened.

Cyber Threats.definition: Malicious software designed to hide its presence and maintain privileged access to a compromised system. Because it can modify the operating system or boot process, a rootkit is very hard to detect and remove, and a full reinstall is sometimes necessary.
Cyber Threats.example: A rootkit hiding malicious processes and files from system monitoring tools.

Cyber Threats.definition: A malicious program or device that records keystrokes to capture sensitive information. Keyloggers can be software installed on the system or small hardware devices attached to a keyboard, and they let attackers collect passwords and card numbers silently.
Cyber Threats.example: A keylogger recording usernames and passwords typed by a victim.

Cyber Threats.definition: A network of compromised devices remotely controlled by an attacker. Botnets are used for DDoS attacks, spam campaigns, credential theft and cryptocurrency mining, and the owners of infected devices are usually unaware.
Cyber Threats.example: Thousands of infected computers being controlled to launch a DDoS attack.

Cyber Threats.definition: A hidden method of bypassing normal authentication or security controls to gain access to a system. Backdoors can be planted by malware or intentionally left by developers, and attackers use them to return to a system later without detection.
Cyber Threats.example: Malware creating a secret remote access mechanism on a compromised computer.

Cyber Threats.definition: Malicious code designed to activate when a specific condition or event occurs. It stays dormant until a trigger such as a date or the deletion of an account occurs, and it is often associated with malicious insiders.
Cyber Threats.example: A program that deletes company files when a particular employee account is removed.

Cyber Threats.definition: The unauthorized use of another person's computing resources to mine cryptocurrency. Victims usually notice slow performance, overheating devices and higher electricity bills, while the attacker profits from the stolen computing power.
Cyber Threats.example: A compromised website secretly using visitors' CPU resources for cryptocurrency mining.

Cyber Threats.definition: Malware that operates primarily in memory or uses legitimate system tools instead of relying on traditional malicious files. Because it leaves very few files on disk, it can bypass traditional antivirus tools and requires behavior-based monitoring to detect.
Cyber Threats.example: An attacker abusing PowerShell to execute malicious commands in memory.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack that obtains the highest administrative privileges on a Linux or Unix-like system. Once root is obtained, the attacker can read or change any file, create accounts and hide traces, so it usually results in a complete system compromise.
Cyber Threats.example: Exploiting a vulnerable service to gain root privileges.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack technique in which an attacker gains higher permissions than originally authorized. It can be vertical (gaining admin rights) or horizontal (accessing another user's data) and often happens after an attacker has gained a low-level foothold.
Cyber Threats.example: A normal user exploiting a vulnerability to obtain administrator privileges.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack that attempts many possible password combinations until the correct one is found. The time needed grows quickly with password length and complexity, so long passwords, account lockout and multi-factor authentication make this attack impractical.
Cyber Threats.example: Repeatedly guessing passwords to gain access to an account.

Cyber Threats.definition: A password attack that tries words and commonly used passwords from a predefined list. It is much faster than trying every combination because many people choose predictable passwords, which is why unique and unusual passphrases are recommended.
Cyber Threats.example: Attempting passwords such as password123 and qwerty.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack that uses stolen username and password combinations to access other accounts. It succeeds because many people reuse the same password on several websites, so using a unique password for each account and enabling MFA greatly reduces the risk.
Cyber Threats.example: Using credentials leaked from one website to access a victim's email account.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack that tries a small number of common passwords against many user accounts. Spreading attempts across many accounts helps the attacker avoid account lockouts, so monitoring for failed logins across many users is an important defense.
Cyber Threats.example: Trying the same weak password against hundreds of employee accounts.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack in which an attacker intercepts or potentially modifies communication between two parties. The attacker may secretly read or alter messages while both parties believe they are talking directly, and encryption with certificate checks helps prevent it.
Cyber Threats.example: An attacker intercepting unencrypted communication between a user and a website.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack that makes a system or service unavailable by overwhelming or disrupting its resources. The goal is to disrupt availability rather than steal data, and it can cause lost revenue and damage to an organization's reputation.
Cyber Threats.example: Flooding a website with excessive requests until it stops responding.

Cyber Threats.definition: A denial-of-service attack launched from multiple devices or systems against a target. Because the traffic comes from thousands of sources, it is hard to block, and defenses include traffic filtering, rate limiting and DDoS protection services.
Cyber Threats.example: A botnet sending massive amounts of traffic to a company's website.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack in which malicious SQL input manipulates database queries due to insufficient input handling. It can allow attackers to read, change or delete database data, and it is prevented by using parameterized queries and validating user input.
Cyber Threats.example: An attacker exploiting a vulnerable login form to bypass authentication.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack in which malicious scripts are injected into web pages and executed in other users' browsers. The script can steal session cookies, redirect users or change page content, and it is prevented by validating input and encoding output.
Cyber Threats.example: A vulnerable comment section displaying an attacker's injected JavaScript.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack that tricks an authenticated user's browser into performing an unwanted action on a website. It works because the browser automatically sends the user's cookies, and it is prevented with anti-CSRF tokens and same-site cookie settings.
Cyber Threats.example: A victim unknowingly submitting a bank transfer request through a malicious webpage.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack that provides false DNS information to redirect users to incorrect or malicious destinations. Because the victim sees a normal-looking address, they may enter passwords on a fake site, and DNSSEC and secure resolvers reduce this risk.
Cyber Threats.example: Redirecting a user from a legitimate banking domain to a fake website.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack in which forged ARP messages associate an attacker's MAC address with another device's IP address. This lets the attacker intercept or modify traffic on the local network, and defenses include dynamic ARP inspection and static ARP entries.
Cyber Threats.example: An attacker impersonating the network gateway on a local network.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack technique in which an attacker forges the source IP address in network packets. It is commonly used in DDoS attacks to hide the attacker's identity and bypass IP-based trust, and ingress and egress filtering helps reduce it.
Cyber Threats.example: Sending packets that appear to originate from a trusted IP address.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack in which an attacker steals or takes control of a user's active session. Attackers may obtain session tokens through sniffing or XSS, so using HTTPS, secure cookies and short session timeouts helps protect users.
Cyber Threats.example: Stealing a session cookie to access a victim's logged-in account.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack in which previously captured communication or authentication data is retransmitted to gain unauthorized access or repeat an action. It works even when the data is encrypted, because the attacker does not need to read it, and defenses include timestamps, nonces and one-time tokens.
Cyber Threats.example: Reusing a captured authentication message to impersonate a legitimate user.

Cyber Threats.definition: A wireless attack in which a fake Wi-Fi access point imitates a legitimate network. Victims who connect to the fake network may have their traffic monitored or be shown fake login pages, so using a VPN and verifying network names is advised.
Cyber Threats.example: A fake airport Wi-Fi hotspot designed to capture users' information.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack that sends forged deauthentication frames to disconnect devices from a wireless network. Attackers often use it to force devices to reconnect so they can capture handshakes or push them onto a fake network, and WPA3 and protected management frames help prevent it.
Cyber Threats.example: Forcing users to disconnect repeatedly from a public Wi-Fi network.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack that exploits a software vulnerability before a security fix is available or before the vulnerability is publicly known to the affected vendor. Because no patch exists, defenders have zero days to prepare, and such exploits are highly valuable and often used in targeted attacks.
Cyber Threats.example: Attackers exploiting a newly discovered browser vulnerability before a patch is released.

Cyber Threats.definition: A vulnerability or attack technique that allows an attacker to execute code on a remote system. It is one of the most severe vulnerability types because it can give attackers full control of a system, and regular patching and input validation reduce the risk.
Cyber Threats.example: Exploiting a vulnerable web application to execute unauthorized commands on its server.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack that manipulates file paths to access files outside the intended directory. Attackers use sequences such as ../ to climb out of the web folder, and the risk is reduced by validating file paths and restricting file access.
Cyber Threats.example: Exploiting a vulnerable website to access its /etc/passwd file.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack that tricks a server into making unauthorized requests to internal or external resources. Because the request comes from a trusted server, it can reach internal systems that are hidden from the Internet, and allow-lists for destinations help prevent it.
Cyber Threats.example: Abusing a vulnerable website to access an internal cloud metadata service.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack that exploits insecure XML processing to access local files or interact with external systems. It can lead to data disclosure, server-side requests or denial of service, and disabling external entity processing in XML parsers prevents it.
Cyber Threats.example: A vulnerable XML parser being manipulated to expose sensitive server files.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack that compromises software, hardware or services through a trusted supplier or third-party component. Since customers trust the supplier, malicious code can reach many organizations at once, and verifying software integrity and vetting vendors help reduce the risk.
Cyber Threats.example: An attacker compromising a software update to distribute malware to customers.

Cyber Threats.definition: A security threat caused by someone within an organization who misuses authorized access, intentionally or accidentally. Insiders already have legitimate access, so the damage can be large, and least-privilege access, monitoring and clear policies help reduce the risk.
Cyber Threats.example: An employee copying confidential company data without permission.

Cyber Threats.definition: A technique that manipulates people into revealing information or performing actions that compromise security. It exploits human trust, curiosity and fear instead of technical flaws, and awareness training is one of the most effective defenses.
Cyber Threats.example: An attacker pretending to be an IT technician to obtain an employee's password.

Cyber Threats.definition: The unauthorized transfer of sensitive information from a system or organization to an external destination. It may happen through malware, email, cloud storage or hidden channels, and data loss prevention tools and network monitoring help detect it.
Cyber Threats.example: An attacker secretly transferring a company's customer database to an external server.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack in which attackers compromise a website frequently visited by their intended victims. The attackers study which sites their targets use and infect those sites with exploits, so even careful users can be compromised through a trusted website.
Cyber Threats.example: Compromising an industry news website to infect employees who regularly visit it.

Cyber Threats.definition: The use of malicious online advertisements to distribute malware or redirect users to harmful websites. Malicious ads can appear on legitimate websites through ad networks and may infect users without any click, so ad blockers and updated software provide protection.
Cyber Threats.example: A fake advertisement redirecting users to a website hosting malicious downloads.

Cyber Threats.definition: A technique that hides data transmission inside DNS queries and responses, sometimes used for command-and-control communication or data theft. Because DNS traffic is usually allowed through firewalls, it can bypass security controls, and monitoring for unusually long or frequent DNS queries helps detect it.
Cyber Threats.example: Malware encoding stolen information into DNS requests to communicate with an attacker-controlled server.

Cyber Threats.definition: A targeted email fraud attack in which criminals impersonate executives, employees or trusted business partners to manipulate financial transactions or steal information. It often involves no malware at all, only convincing messages, and it causes large financial losses, so verifying payment requests through a second channel is important.
Cyber Threats.example: An attacker impersonating a company's CEO and requesting an urgent bank transfer.

Cyber Threats.definition: Short for malicious software, it is any program designed to damage, disrupt or gain unauthorized access to systems or data. Viruses, worms, trojans and ransomware are all types of malware.
Cyber Threats.example: A downloaded program that secretly steals saved passwords.

Cyber Threats.definition: Malware that frightens users with fake warnings about viruses or problems to trick them into buying useless or harmful software.
Cyber Threats.example: A pop-up claiming "Your PC is infected!" and urging a paid cleanup.

Cyber Threats.definition: A criminal business model where ransomware developers rent their malware to affiliates who carry out attacks and share the profits. It lets people with little skill launch ransomware campaigns.
Cyber Threats.example: An affiliate using a rented ransomware kit to attack a hospital.

Cyber Threats.definition: Malware designed to permanently destroy data or make systems unusable instead of seeking payment. It is often used in sabotage and cyber warfare.
Cyber Threats.example: Malware erasing the hard drives of a company's computers.

Cyber Threats.definition: A type of rootkit that infects the boot process, such as the master boot record, so it loads before the operating system. This makes it very hard to detect and remove.
Cyber Threats.example: Malware modifying the boot sector to run before Windows starts.

Cyber Threats.definition: Malware that changes its code or appearance each time it spreads to avoid signature-based antivirus detection, while keeping the same function.
Cyber Threats.example: A virus encrypting itself with a new key for every infection.

Cyber Threats.definition: Malware that rewrites its own code completely with each new copy, rather than only changing the encryption. This makes detection even harder.
Cyber Threats.example: A virus that rearranges its instructions every time it replicates.

Cyber Threats.definition: A virus written in the macro language of applications like word processors and spreadsheets. It runs when a user opens an infected document and enables macros.
Cyber Threats.example: A Word file that asks you to "Enable Content" and then downloads malware.

Cyber Threats.definition: A virus that infects the boot sector of a drive and runs when the computer starts. It was common in the era of floppy disks and still shows up in modern bootkits.
Cyber Threats.example: An infected USB drive spreading a virus when the PC boots from it.

Cyber Threats.definition: A trojan that gives an attacker remote control over an infected computer, including access to files, the webcam and the keyboard.
Cyber Threats.example: A fake game installer secretly letting an attacker view the victim's screen.

Cyber Threats.definition: Malware designed to steal online banking credentials and financial information, often by showing fake login forms or capturing keystrokes.
Cyber Threats.example: A trojan overlaying a fake form on a bank's login page.

Cyber Threats.definition: A malicious program whose job is to install or "drop" other malware onto a system. The dropper itself may look harmless to avoid detection.
Cyber Threats.example: A small file that installs a keylogger after running.

Cyber Threats.definition: A small piece of malware that downloads and runs additional malicious components from the Internet. It helps attackers deliver a larger payload in stages.
Cyber Threats.example: Malware that contacts a server and downloads ransomware.

Cyber Threats.definition: The part of malware or an exploit that performs the harmful action, such as deleting files, encrypting data or opening a backdoor.
Cyber Threats.example: The code that encrypts files after a ransomware infection.

Cyber Threats.definition: A toolkit that automatically scans a victim's browser or software for vulnerabilities and uses them to install malware. It is often delivered through compromised websites or ads.
Cyber Threats.example: A malicious ad redirecting a visitor to a page that tests for browser flaws.

Cyber Threats.definition: Malware that collects sensitive data such as saved passwords, cookies, cryptocurrency wallets and system details, and sends it to attackers.
Cyber Threats.example: A program stealing browser-saved passwords and sending them to a server.

Cyber Threats.definition: Malicious software targeting smartphones and tablets, often spread through fake apps, malicious links or text messages.
Cyber Threats.example: A fake flashlight app that reads text messages.

Cyber Threats.definition: Software secretly installed on a device to monitor someone's location, messages and activity without their knowledge. It is a serious privacy and safety threat.
Cyber Threats.example: An app hidden on a phone that tracks the owner's location.

Cyber Threats.definition: Malware or an unwanted extension that changes browser settings such as the homepage or search engine to redirect users to certain sites.
Cyber Threats.example: A browser suddenly using a strange search engine after installing free software.

Cyber Threats.definition: Software that may not be strictly malicious but is unwanted, such as bundled toolbars or system optimizers. It often installs with free programs and can reduce security.
Cyber Threats.example: A free PDF tool installing extra toolbars without clear consent.

Cyber Threats.definition: The infrastructure attackers use to communicate with and give instructions to compromised systems. Infected devices connect to it to receive commands and send stolen data.
Cyber Threats.example: Malware checking a server every minute for new instructions.

Cyber Threats.definition: A compromised computer that is controlled remotely by an attacker, often as part of a botnet, without the owner's knowledge.
Cyber Threats.example: A home PC secretly sending spam as part of a botnet.

Cyber Threats.definition: Unsolicited bulk messages, usually email, sent in large numbers for advertising, scams or to spread malware.
Cyber Threats.example: Thousands of emails offering a fake prize with a malicious link.

Cyber Threats.definition: The automatic download and installation of malware when a user simply visits a compromised website, often by exploiting browser vulnerabilities, with no clicking needed.
Cyber Threats.example: Visiting a hacked blog that silently installs a trojan.

Cyber Threats.definition: A prolonged, targeted cyberattack in which a skilled group gains access to a network and stays hidden for a long time to steal data or spy. APTs are often linked to nation-states.
Cyber Threats.example: A group spending months inside a government network to steal documents.

Cyber Threats.definition: A technique in which attackers use legitimate tools already present in the system, such as PowerShell or WMI, instead of bringing their own malware, which makes detection difficult.
Cyber Threats.example: An attacker using built-in Windows tools to run commands and move around.

Cyber Threats.definition: A technique where malicious code is inserted into the memory of a legitimate running process so it runs under that process's identity and avoids detection.
Cyber Threats.example: Malware injecting code into explorer.exe to hide.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack that tricks a program into loading a malicious dynamic link library instead of the legitimate one by placing it where the program looks first.
Cyber Threats.example: A malicious DLL placed in an application's folder gets loaded instead of the real one.

Cyber Threats.definition: The techniques attackers use to move from one compromised system to others inside a network while searching for valuable data and higher privileges.
Cyber Threats.example: An attacker using stolen credentials to log in to other servers on the network.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack in which an attacker inserts malicious code into a program or process, which the application then executes as if it were legitimate.
Cyber Threats.example: Injecting script code into an application that evaluates user input.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack that compromises a device without any interaction from the victim, such as opening a message or clicking a link. It is especially dangerous and difficult to detect.
Cyber Threats.example: A malicious message that compromises a phone as soon as it is received.

Cyber Threats.definition: A method malware or attackers use to stay on a system after a reboot or logout, such as startup entries, scheduled tasks or services.
Cyber Threats.example: Malware adding itself to the Windows Run registry key.

Cyber Threats.definition: A vulnerability in which a program writes more data to a memory buffer than it can hold, overwriting adjacent memory. Attackers can use it to crash programs or run their own code.
Cyber Threats.example: Sending a very long input to a C program that uses gets().

Cyber Threats.definition: A buffer overflow that happens in the heap, the memory area used for dynamic allocation. It can corrupt data structures and may lead to code execution.
Cyber Threats.example: Writing beyond the end of a block allocated with malloc().

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack that exploits functions like printf when user input is used directly as the format string, allowing attackers to read memory or write to it.
Cyber Threats.example: Entering %x%x%x into a vulnerable program to leak memory values.

Cyber Threats.definition: A flaw where an arithmetic operation produces a value too large for the data type, wrapping around and causing unexpected behavior such as incorrect memory allocation.
Cyber Threats.example: An unsigned 8-bit value of 255 becoming 0 after adding 1.

Cyber Threats.definition: A flaw that occurs when the outcome of a program depends on the timing of events, which an attacker can manipulate to gain unintended access.
Cyber Threats.example: Changing a file between a program's permission check and its use.

Cyber Threats.definition: A memory corruption bug where a program continues to use memory after it has been freed, which attackers can exploit to run malicious code.
Cyber Threats.example: A browser bug where a freed object is accessed again.

Cyber Threats.definition: An exploitation technique that chains small pieces of existing code, called gadgets, to perform malicious actions and bypass protections that block injected code.
Cyber Threats.example: An attacker chaining existing instructions to bypass non-executable memory.

Cyber Threats.definition: A small piece of machine code used as the payload in an exploit, traditionally to start a command shell on the target.
Cyber Threats.example: Code injected through a buffer overflow that spawns a shell.

Cyber Threats.definition: A shell in which the compromised machine connects back to the attacker, which helps bypass firewalls that block incoming connections.
Cyber Threats.example: A victim's computer connecting out to an attacker's listener.

Cyber Threats.definition: A shell in which the compromised machine opens a port and waits for the attacker to connect to it. It is often blocked by firewalls on inbound traffic.
Cyber Threats.example: A target listening on port 4444 for the attacker's connection.

Cyber Threats.definition: A malicious script uploaded to a web server that gives attackers remote control through a web interface. It is a common way to keep access after a breach.
Cyber Threats.example: A hidden PHP file allowing an attacker to run commands on a server.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack where an attacker makes an application run arbitrary operating system commands by inserting them into input that is passed to a system shell.
Cyber Threats.example: Entering ; cat /etc/passwd into a vulnerable ping form.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack that manipulates LDAP queries by inserting malicious input, potentially bypassing authentication or exposing directory data.
Cyber Threats.example: Using special characters in a login field to alter an LDAP search filter.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack that manipulates queries to NoSQL databases such as MongoDB by supplying malicious input, which may bypass logins or reveal data.
Cyber Threats.example: Sending a JSON operator in a login request to bypass a password check.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack that alters XPath queries used to read XML data by inserting malicious input, which can expose or bypass data.
Cyber Threats.example: Entering ' or '1'='1 into a field used in an XPath query.

Cyber Threats.definition: A type of SQL injection where the application does not display database errors or results, so attackers infer information from behavior or timing.
Cyber Threats.example: Asking true or false questions through page responses to extract data.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack where an attacker inserts HTML code into a web page through input that is not properly handled, which can change how the page looks or trick users.
Cyber Threats.example: A comment containing a fake login form that appears on the page.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack that manipulates the HTTP Host header to poison links, caches or password reset emails if the application trusts it blindly.
Cyber Threats.example: Changing the Host header so a reset email contains an attacker's link.

Cyber Threats.definition: A vulnerability where an application accepts untrusted serialized data and rebuilds objects from it, which can lead to code execution or tampering.
Cyber Threats.example: Modifying a serialized object in a cookie to gain admin rights.

Cyber Threats.definition: Weaknesses in login or session handling that let attackers compromise passwords, session tokens or accounts, such as weak password rules or exposed session IDs.
Cyber Threats.example: A site allowing unlimited login attempts without lockout.

Cyber Threats.definition: A vulnerability in which users can act outside their intended permissions, such as viewing other people's data or reaching admin functions.
Cyber Threats.example: A normal user opening an admin page by typing its URL.

Cyber Threats.definition: A flaw where an application exposes internal identifiers and lets users access other people's data by changing them.
Cyber Threats.example: Changing /invoice?id=101 to id=102 and seeing another customer's invoice.

Cyber Threats.definition: Insecure settings such as default passwords, open ports, unnecessary services or detailed error messages that make a system easier to attack.
Cyber Threats.example: A database left online with the default administrator password.

Cyber Threats.definition: The failure to adequately protect sensitive information like passwords, card numbers or health records, for example by not encrypting it.
Cyber Threats.example: A website storing passwords in plain text.

Cyber Threats.definition: A vulnerability where a website redirects users to a URL supplied by the attacker without validation. It is used to make phishing links look trustworthy.
Cyber Threats.example: A trusted site link that redirects visitors to a fake login page.

Cyber Threats.definition: A vulnerability that lets an attacker include files from the server's own filesystem through a vulnerable parameter, possibly exposing sensitive data or running code.
Cyber Threats.example: Using ?page=../../etc/passwd to display a system file.

Cyber Threats.definition: A vulnerability where an application loads and runs a file from an external server specified by the attacker, which can result in remote code execution.
Cyber Threats.example: Pointing a page parameter to a malicious script on another website.

Cyber Threats.definition: A flaw where a website allows files of dangerous types to be uploaded without proper checks, letting attackers upload malicious scripts.
Cyber Threats.example: Uploading a PHP web shell disguised as an image.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack that exploits differences in how front-end and back-end servers interpret HTTP requests, letting attackers sneak hidden requests through.
Cyber Threats.example: Sending a request with conflicting length headers to bypass security controls.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack that supplies multiple parameters with the same name to confuse how a web application or filter processes them.
Cyber Threats.example: Sending ?id=1&id=2 to bypass input validation.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack that tricks a user into clicking something different from what they see, usually by hiding a page inside a transparent frame.
Cyber Threats.example: A hidden frame making a user click "Like" or "Delete" unknowingly.

Cyber Threats.definition: An insecure Cross-Origin Resource Sharing policy that lets untrusted websites read sensitive responses from another site in a user's browser.
Cyber Threats.example: A server allowing any origin to access private account data.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack where an attacker claims an unused external service that a subdomain still points to, gaining control of that subdomain.
Cyber Threats.example: blog.example.com pointing to a deleted hosting account that an attacker registers.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack that changes DNS settings or responses so users are redirected to malicious servers, for example by altering router DNS settings or compromising a registrar.
Cyber Threats.example: A router's DNS changed so banking sites open a fake page.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack that inserts false data into a DNS resolver's cache so users are directed to malicious sites.
Cyber Threats.example: A resolver storing a wrong IP address for a bank's domain.

Cyber Threats.definition: A DDoS technique that sends small DNS requests with a spoofed source address so large DNS responses flood the victim.
Cyber Threats.example: Attackers using open resolvers to send huge responses to a target.

Cyber Threats.definition: A DoS attack that sends many TCP SYN requests without completing the handshake, exhausting the server's connection resources.
Cyber Threats.example: Sending thousands of SYN packets from fake addresses to a web server.

Cyber Threats.definition: A DoS attack that sends a large number of UDP packets to random ports, overwhelming the target and its network.
Cyber Threats.example: A target flooded with UDP traffic until it becomes unresponsive.

Cyber Threats.definition: A DoS attack that overwhelms a target with a flood of ICMP packets such as ping requests.
Cyber Threats.example: Sending continuous large pings to saturate a server's bandwidth.

Cyber Threats.definition: An old attack that sent oversized or malformed ICMP packets that could crash vulnerable systems. Modern systems are generally protected.
Cyber Threats.example: Sending an oversized ping packet to crash an old operating system.

Cyber Threats.definition: A DDoS attack that sends ICMP echo requests to a broadcast address with the victim's spoofed IP, so many devices reply to the victim.
Cyber Threats.example: A broadcast ping causing hundreds of replies to flood a victim.

Cyber Threats.definition: A DoS attack that holds many connections to a web server open by sending partial HTTP requests very slowly, exhausting its connection capacity.
Cyber Threats.example: A web server unable to accept new visitors because slow connections occupy all slots.

Cyber Threats.definition: A DDoS attack that overwhelms a web server with many seemingly legitimate HTTP requests, which makes it difficult to distinguish from normal traffic.
Cyber Threats.example: A botnet repeatedly requesting a heavy search page.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack that sends fragmented packets with overlapping offsets, causing some older systems to crash when reassembling them.
Cyber Threats.example: Overlapping IP fragments crashing an unpatched system.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack that floods a switch with fake MAC addresses until its address table is full, causing it to broadcast traffic so attackers can eavesdrop.
Cyber Threats.example: Sending thousands of fake frames to make a switch behave like a hub.

Cyber Threats.definition: Changing a device's MAC address to impersonate another device or bypass MAC-based access controls.
Cyber Threats.example: Cloning an authorized laptop's MAC address to join a restricted network.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack that lets a device send traffic to a VLAN it should not access, for example through switch spoofing or double tagging.
Cyber Threats.example: An attacker on one VLAN reaching devices on another.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack that requests all available IP addresses from a DHCP server using fake MAC addresses, so legitimate clients cannot obtain addresses.
Cyber Threats.example: A flood of DHCP requests leaving no addresses for new devices.

Cyber Threats.definition: An unauthorized DHCP server on a network that gives clients malicious settings, such as a fake gateway or DNS server, to redirect traffic.
Cyber Threats.example: A malicious device handing out itself as the default gateway.

Cyber Threats.definition: An unauthorized wireless access point connected to a network, which can create a hidden entry point for attackers.
Cyber Threats.example: An employee plugging in a cheap router that bypasses security.

Cyber Threats.definition: Sending unsolicited messages to nearby Bluetooth-enabled devices. It is mostly an annoyance but can be used for social engineering.
Cyber Threats.example: An anonymous message appearing on a phone in a crowded place.

Cyber Threats.definition: Unauthorized access to information on a Bluetooth device, such as contacts or messages, by exploiting vulnerabilities.
Cyber Threats.example: An attacker nearby copying a phone's contact list over Bluetooth.

Cyber Threats.definition: The Key Reinstallation Attack exploits a flaw in the WPA2 four-way handshake to decrypt Wi-Fi traffic by forcing key reuse. It was discovered in 2017 and fixed by patches.
Cyber Threats.example: An attacker forcing a device to reinstall an encryption key and read its data.

Cyber Threats.definition: The act of searching for Wi-Fi networks while moving, usually with a laptop or phone, to map networks and find insecure ones.
Cyber Threats.example: Driving through a city and logging unprotected Wi-Fi networks.

Cyber Threats.definition: The deliberate use of radio interference to disrupt Wi-Fi or other wireless signals and make the service unavailable.
Cyber Threats.example: A device flooding a frequency so nearby Wi-Fi stops working.

Cyber Threats.definition: The process of probing a host to find which ports are open and which services are running. Attackers use it for reconnaissance, and defenders use it for audits.
Cyber Threats.example: Running a scanner to find that ports 22 and 80 are open.

Cyber Threats.definition: The reconnaissance phase of gathering information about a target, such as domain names, IP ranges and employee details, before an attack.
Cyber Threats.example: Collecting a company's public DNS records and email formats.

Cyber Threats.definition: Open Source Intelligence is information collected from publicly available sources such as websites, social media and public records. Attackers and defenders both use it.
Cyber Threats.example: Finding an employee's job title on a professional networking site.

Cyber Threats.definition: A technique for collecting information about a service, such as its name and version, from the message it shows when a connection is made.
Cyber Threats.example: Connecting to a mail server and reading its version banner.

Cyber Threats.definition: The automated process of checking systems and applications for known security weaknesses. It helps prioritize patches.
Cyber Threats.example: Running a scanner that reports outdated software on servers.

Cyber Threats.definition: The process of actively extracting details from a target, such as user names, shares and services, after initial reconnaissance.
Cyber Threats.example: Listing user accounts on a server through an exposed service.

Cyber Threats.definition: A social engineering technique in which an attacker invents a believable story or identity to obtain information from a victim.
Cyber Threats.example: Someone posing as an auditor to request employee records.

Cyber Threats.definition: A social engineering attack that lures victims with something attractive, such as a free download or a USB drive left in public, to deliver malware.
Cyber Threats.example: A USB drive labeled "Salary Details" left in a parking lot.

Cyber Threats.definition: Gaining physical access to a restricted area by closely following an authorized person through a secured door.
Cyber Threats.example: An intruder walking into an office behind an employee who swiped a card.

Cyber Threats.definition: A social engineering attack that offers a service or benefit in exchange for information or access.
Cyber Threats.example: A caller pretending to be technical support offering help in return for login details.

Cyber Threats.definition: Watching someone enter sensitive information, such as a PIN or password, by looking over their shoulder or using a camera.
Cyber Threats.example: A person watching a victim enter a PIN at an ATM.

Cyber Threats.definition: Searching through discarded materials to find sensitive information such as documents, notes or old devices.
Cyber Threats.example: Finding printed passwords in an office trash bin.

Cyber Threats.definition: Registering domain names that are slight misspellings of popular websites to catch users who make typing mistakes, often for phishing or malware.
Cyber Threats.example: Registering gogle.com to trick people looking for google.com.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack that redirects users from a legitimate website to a fake one, often by corrupting DNS or local host files, even when they type the correct address.
Cyber Threats.example: Typing a real bank URL and landing on a fake copy.

Cyber Threats.definition: A phishing attack that copies a legitimate, previously delivered email and replaces its link or attachment with a malicious one.
Cyber Threats.example: A resend of a real invoice email with an infected attachment.

Cyber Threats.definition: The collection of usernames and passwords, usually through fake login pages or phishing, to be used or sold later.
Cyber Threats.example: A fake cloud storage login page recording submitted passwords.

Cyber Threats.definition: AI-generated or AI-altered audio, images or video that realistically imitate real people. It is used for fraud, impersonation and misinformation.
Cyber Threats.example: A fake voice call imitating a company executive to request a payment.

Cyber Threats.definition: Forging the sender address of an email so it appears to come from a trusted source. SPF, DKIM and DMARC help detect it.
Cyber Threats.example: An email that seems to come from the CEO but was sent by an attacker.

Cyber Threats.definition: Phishing that uses QR codes to lead victims to malicious websites. Users scan the code without being able to see the full link.
Cyber Threats.example: A fake parking payment QR sticker leading to a scam site.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack where criminals persuade a mobile carrier to transfer a victim's phone number to a SIM they control, so they can receive verification codes.
Cyber Threats.example: An attacker taking over a number to intercept a bank's one-time password.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack in which an attacker uses a stolen password hash to authenticate without knowing the actual password, mainly in Windows environments.
Cyber Threats.example: Using a captured NTLM hash to log in to another server.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack that uses stolen Kerberos tickets to impersonate a user and access resources without knowing the password.
Cyber Threats.example: Reusing a stolen Kerberos ticket to access a file server.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack in which an attacker requests Kerberos service tickets for service accounts and cracks them offline to recover the account passwords.
Cyber Threats.example: Cracking a service account's ticket to learn its weak password.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack in which an attacker forges Kerberos tickets using the krbtgt account's secret, giving long-lasting and wide access to a domain.
Cyber Threats.example: An attacker creating tickets that grant domain administrator access.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack that uses precomputed tables of password hashes to quickly reverse hashes into passwords. Salting passwords defeats it.
Cyber Threats.example: Looking up an unsalted hash in a large table to find the password.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack that exploits two different inputs producing the same hash value, which can undermine integrity checks and digital signatures.
Cyber Threats.example: Creating two different documents with the same MD5 hash.

Cyber Threats.definition: A cryptographic attack based on the birthday paradox, which finds collisions in hash functions far faster than expected.
Cyber Threats.example: Finding two messages with the same hash after far fewer attempts than brute force.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack that reprograms a USB device to behave as another device, such as a keyboard, and send malicious keystrokes automatically.
Cyber Threats.example: A USB stick that types commands once plugged in.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack that recovers encryption keys or data from a computer's memory shortly after it is powered off or restarted, since RAM retains data briefly.
Cyber Threats.example: Rebooting a laptop from a USB drive to read its memory contents.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack that exploits physical access to an unattended device to install malicious software or tamper with its boot process.
Cyber Threats.example: Someone modifying a laptop's bootloader while it is left in a hotel room.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack that gains information from the physical behavior of a system, such as timing, power use or sound, instead of attacking the algorithm itself.
Cyber Threats.example: Measuring how long a login check takes to guess a secret.

Cyber Threats.definition: A family of CPU vulnerabilities that exploit speculative execution to leak data between programs. They were disclosed in 2018 and affect many processors.
Cyber Threats.example: A malicious program reading memory belonging to another process through the CPU cache.

Cyber Threats.definition: A CPU vulnerability that lets an unprivileged process read kernel memory by abusing out-of-order execution. It was disclosed in 2018 together with Spectre.
Cyber Threats.example: A program reading protected kernel memory on an unpatched processor.

Cyber Threats.definition: A hardware attack that repeatedly accesses rows of memory so electrical interference flips bits in neighboring rows, which can break security.
Cyber Threats.example: Repeated memory access causing a bit to flip and change permissions.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack that forces a system to use an older, weaker protocol or encryption version that is easier to break.
Cyber Threats.example: Forcing a connection to fall back from TLS 1.3 to an insecure version.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack that downgrades a victim's HTTPS connection to HTTP by intercepting traffic, so the attacker can read data in plain text.
Cyber Threats.example: A user on public Wi-Fi unknowingly using HTTP for a banking site.

Cyber Threats.definition: A cryptographic attack that uses error messages about padding to decrypt data without knowing the key.
Cyber Threats.example: A server's different errors for bad padding being used to decrypt a cookie.

Cyber Threats.definition: A serious 2014 vulnerability in the OpenSSL library that let attackers read memory from servers, potentially exposing private keys and passwords.
Cyber Threats.example: Requesting extra data from a vulnerable server and receiving memory contents.

Cyber Threats.definition: A 2014 vulnerability in the Bash shell that allowed attackers to run commands through specially crafted environment variables.
Cyber Threats.example: Sending a malicious header to a CGI script to run commands on the server.

Cyber Threats.definition: A critical 2021 vulnerability in the Apache Log4j library that allowed remote code execution through crafted log messages.
Cyber Threats.example: Sending a special string to a server that logged it using Log4j.

Cyber Threats.definition: An exploit for a vulnerability in Microsoft's SMBv1 protocol that allowed remote code execution. It was used by the WannaCry ransomware.
Cyber Threats.example: WannaCry spreading to unpatched Windows computers through SMB.

Cyber Threats.definition: A botnet that infected Internet of Things devices using default passwords and launched massive DDoS attacks, notably in 2016.
Cyber Threats.example: Infected cameras and routers flooding a DNS provider with traffic.

Cyber Threats.definition: A sophisticated worm discovered in 2010 that targeted industrial control systems and was used to damage uranium enrichment centrifuges.
Cyber Threats.example: A worm that altered the behavior of specific industrial controllers.

Cyber Threats.definition: An incident in which sensitive, protected or confidential data is accessed or disclosed without authorization.
Cyber Threats.example: Attackers stealing customer records from an online store.

Cyber Threats.definition: The accidental exposure of sensitive data caused by error or poor security rather than a deliberate attack.
Cyber Threats.example: A database exposed online because it had no password.

Cyber Threats.definition: The use of someone else's personal information, such as a national ID or bank details, to commit fraud or other crimes.
Cyber Threats.example: Opening a loan using a victim's stolen personal details.

Cyber Threats.definition: A situation in which an attacker gains control of a legitimate user's account, often using stolen or guessed credentials.
Cyber Threats.example: An attacker logging in to a victim's email using a leaked password.

Cyber Threats.definition: Publishing someone's private or identifying information online without permission, often to harass or intimidate them.
Cyber Threats.example: Posting a person's home address on social media to harass them.

Cyber Threats.definition: Using the Internet or electronic means to repeatedly harass, monitor or threaten an individual.
Cyber Threats.example: Sending constant threatening messages and tracking someone's accounts.

Cyber Threats.definition: Generating fake clicks on online advertisements to drain advertising budgets or earn fraudulent revenue.
Cyber Threats.example: A bot repeatedly clicking an ad to waste a competitor's budget.

Cyber Threats.definition: Stealing payment card details using a hidden device placed on a card reader, such as an ATM or fuel pump.
Cyber Threats.example: A tiny device attached to an ATM that copies card data.

Cyber Threats.definition: Injecting malicious code into online payment forms to steal card details as customers enter them.
Cyber Threats.example: Malicious script on a checkout page sending card numbers to an attacker.

Cyber Threats.definition: The use of stolen credit card details to buy goods or test cards, often in large automated amounts.
Cyber Threats.example: Testing thousands of stolen card numbers with small purchases.

Cyber Threats.definition: Cloud storage set with overly permissive access so that private data can be viewed or downloaded by anyone.
Cyber Threats.example: A publicly accessible storage bucket containing customer files.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attacker taking control of a cloud service account, which can give access to data, resources and the ability to run malicious workloads.
Cyber Threats.example: Stolen cloud credentials used to launch costly mining servers.

Cyber Threats.definition: Misuse of an application programming interface, such as exploiting weak authentication, missing limits or logic flaws to access data or disrupt service.
Cyber Threats.example: Scraping private user data from an API that has no rate limiting.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack in which code running inside a container breaks out to access the host system or other containers.
Cyber Threats.example: Exploiting a vulnerability to gain control of the host from within a container.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack on AI language model applications in which malicious instructions in input or documents cause the model to ignore its intended rules or reveal data.
Cyber Threats.example: A web page containing hidden instructions that manipulate an AI assistant.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack that corrupts the data used to train a machine learning model so the model learns incorrect or malicious behavior.
Cyber Threats.example: Adding mislabeled examples to a dataset to make a spam filter fail.

Cyber Threats.definition: An attack that uses carefully crafted inputs to make a machine learning model give wrong results, often with changes humans cannot notice.
Cyber Threats.example: A slightly altered image causing a model to misidentify a stop sign.

Cyber Threats.definition: A supply chain attack in which an attacker publishes a malicious public package with the same name as a company's private package so build tools install it instead.
Cyber Threats.example: A build system downloading a public package that has the same name as an internal one.

Cyber Threats.definition: A browser add-on that appears useful but secretly steals data, injects ads or tracks activity.
Cyber Threats.example: A free coupon extension recording the sites a user visits.

Cyber Threats.definition: The use of hacking to promote a political or social cause, often through website defacement, data leaks or DDoS attacks.
Cyber Threats.example: A group defacing a government website to protest a policy.
